companies.company: Hims UK (with Hers UK for women)
companies.parent: Hims & Hers Health, Inc. (US). UK contracting company: Hims & Hers UK Limited. The site, clinicians and pharmacy are now run by Fill Function UK Limited, the UK arm of Eucalyptus (the Juniper and Pilot platform), described by Hims as 'part of the same group of companies'.
companies.model: Subscription telehealth: a long marketing quiz, a medical questionnaire reviewed by a UK clinician without a call, then compounded finasteride and minoxidil products (sprays, serum, chews) or generics posted every 1 to 12 months, paid up front.
companies.accountWall: Men (Hims): after 21 anonymous screens, at https://app.forhims.co.uk/start/signup?t=hair&anon_flow_key=hair — 'Ready to see if you’re eligible? Next we'll cover your health and medical history as well as treatment options.' asks for an email address. Nothing medical, no product and no price has been shown by then; the last thing before the wall is a fixed 'Great news—we have options that may work for you', an answer summary and marketing screens. Women (Hers): at the first screen (first and last name).
companies.coverageNote: Stage 1 (map) walked the whole anonymous men's quiz and read the served quiz definition, product and price tables, app code and public documents. Stage 2 (experiment) replayed the baseline twice and then changed one answer at a time: 31 runs covering every non-baseline option of all 11 anonymous questions, so all 42 options have now been clicked live. Seven further runs checked two multi-select combinations, the phone layout, a returning visitor, skipping the quiz, two other landing pages and the Hers entry: 40 replays in all. Every run kept the full server traffic, which showed the server choosing the next step after each answer and returning no result at the end. Stage 2 also read ten more of the app's code files (how the server's eligibility result is used, the consent screen, brand settings) and the older Hims UK help centre (vitamin strengths in the chews). Not obtained, and not obtainable without an account: the wording of the medical questions, the rules that map answers to products, any live recommendation, and the checkout prices. Nothing at all could be tested on Hers UK, which asks for a name first.
companies.engineSummary: Hims UK's engine has two parts, and only the first can be watched from outside. Part one is a marketing quiz anyone can take: 11 questions (intent, where, how much, when, goals, hair type, hair length, family history, stress, styling, time) with 10 selling screens between them. Stage 2 changed every answer one at a time (31 replays covering all 42 options) and the engine did not move: same screens, same order, same 'Great news—we have options that may work for you', same email wall. Six answers are repeated on one summary screen; the other five are never shown again. No answer stops anyone, warns anyone, or shows a product, strength or price. The server traffic agrees: after each answer the server names the next step, and at the end it returns a record id and nothing else. If the visitor signs up, his stored answers are attached to the new account. Part two sits behind the account: date of birth, a medical questionnaire, then a server-side rules step that marks each of ten products eligible or not and names one as the recommendation. A patient the server calls 'not eligible' sees a rejection screen. Everyone else sees one recommended product, with the other nine a tap away and the ruled-out ones greyed out as 'Not available based on your medical history'. The 'Selected based on your goals' chips on each product page are fixed text, not built from his answers. He then picks a plan length, ticks a consent box, gives GP details and pays up front; a clinician reviews the answers without a call and approves or refunds. The wording of the medical questions and the answer-to-product rules are not public. The best guides to them are Hims's own leaflets (who must not use each product) and the old platform's tag system, in which an answer could exclude every product tagged 'finasteride', 'minoxidil-oral', 'topical' and so on. Hers UK runs on the same platform with five minoxidil-based treatments for women, but asks for a name on the first screen, so nothing there can be tested without an account.
topOpportunities: Give a real answer before asking for contact details: likely pattern, which treatments fit, which are ruled out and why, and the price. Hims asks 11 questions and returns nothing

Make the quiz respond. Not one of Hims's 42 options changes anything on screen. React at once: sudden or patchy loss → 'see a GP first'; shaved head or a hat every day → suggest tablets; heavy stress with no family history → explain shedding and offer a blood test
Ask the safety questions early (blood pressure, heart, mood, fertility plans, current medicines) and say in plain words when and why a product is ruled out, instead of a greyed-out card after sign-up

companies.parent: Menwell Limited (its hair-loss service traded as Manual before moving to the Voy brand; exact date of the move not checked)
companies.model: UK subscription telehealth: online quiz, remote prescriber review, own distance-selling pharmacy; sells licensed finasteride plus own-brand unlicensed specials (10% minoxidil spray, combined finasteride or dutasteride + minoxidil capsules, topical combination spray) and add-on shampoo and vitamins.
companies.accountWall: The real consultation was never reached (security checkpoint before the first question), so the exact place of the sign-in step is not seen. Older app code puts it after the anonymous quiz, the recommendation, the format and plan-length choice and the add-ons, at /checkout/email ('Create an account': first name, last name, email, phone number, date of birth, password), followed by a medical-history questionnaire, hair photos and the order review. On both landing-page pop-ups (men and women) the wall is an email box straight after one picture question: the 'eligible / not eligible' verdict is only shown after an email is given. Voy's help-centre articles also need sign-in.
companies.coverageNote: No real quiz screen was seen, in stage 1 or stage 2. Live replays (20 in stage 2, 3 of them blocked access checks) cover only what Voy serves without the checkpoint: the men's landing-page pop-up (6 options), the women's landing-page pop-up (4 options and Skip) and the men's pattern picker (6 options), each option on its own. Site code covers (a) the scripts of those landing pages, which hold the pop-ups' eligibility rule, and (b) a copy of the older Manual web app's shared script (29 Dec 2025, from a public web archive), which holds the quiz ENGINE (how answers remove products or reject the patient, how follow-up questions are shown, the order of the funnel pages) but not the questions. Public documents cover Voy's own landing pages for men and women (read live on Voy's public hosts hairloss1.joinvoy.com and femalehairloss1.joinvoy.com), older Manual treatment-plan pages with full 'who should not take it' lists (archive copies), terms of sale, GPhC reports and Manual's published service evaluation. Help-centre and www.joinvoy.com product pages were read only through search-engine summaries. Every quiz-related entry says which of these it rests on. Stage 3 (verification) replayed every baseline and six stage 2 experiments again with the same results, re-read the page scripts and the archived app code, and added 13 gap replays: the older Manual plan picker that is still online (format and plan length, the only product chooser that works without the blocked app), the page aimed at both sexes, the women's /meta pop-up, the product-first landing page and the coupon hand-over. None of these is the consultation itself.
companies.engineSummary: Voy's real quiz could not be opened in any of the three stages, so this is the engine only as far as public evidence shows it. What was seen: (1) A pattern gate before the quiz. The men's and women's landing pages open a one-question pop-up. Its own script refuses 'Patchy' and 'Complete' (men) and 'Patchy hair loss' (women) with 'You aren't eligible', and sends everyone else to the quiz with a discount code attached. The verdict only appears after an email is given; ticking a refused option looks exactly like ticking an accepted one. The page aimed at both sexes shows the men's picture question to everyone. A separate pattern picker is pure marketing: every pattern leads to the same quiz link. (2) On an older Manual page that is still online, choosing 'Spray' instead of 'Tablets' switches the product (minoxidil capsules to 10% spray) at the same price, and choosing 3 months instead of 6 changes only the price and pack size. What was read in code, not seen running: an 11-month-old copy of the same web app (Manual, December 2025). There the quiz starts with a list of products, and each question can carry a reject list (one matching answer leaves no product and shows 'You aren't eligible', with a 'Review your answers' button), an exclude list (the answer removes named products and the quiz carries on) and parent or JSON Logic conditions (the answer opens, hides or rewords later questions). In that function an answer can only remove products, never add one. Which answers sit on which list is in a definition the app downloads at run time; it could not be read, and that code has no women's hair flow in it. What Voy publishes: lists of who should not have which medicine. DHT blockers (finasteride, dutasteride) are 'not suitable' for men trying for a baby or with a pregnant partner, men treated for an enlarged prostate, men who have had breast or prostate cancer, and men with severe depression; minoxidil 'should not be used' with low or uncontrolled blood pressure or a sore scalp, or over 65; under-18s, women (in the men's service) and men who are completely bald or do not have pattern hair loss are not treated. Whether the quiz applies each of these by removing a product, by warning, or by leaving it to the clinician was not seen. After the quiz, older code and Voy's pages point to: a recommendation (Voy leads with finasteride plus minoxidil together for men; women are offered minoxidil only, as serum or tablets, at a strength the clinician sets), a format and plan-length choice, add-ons (shampoo, vitamins), then the account, a medical-history questionnaire, photos and payment details, and a prescriber's review that sees flagged and changed answers. Older terms say payment is taken only on approval.
companies.verdict: Trust this report for three things: (1) what Voy shows in public before the quiz (the pop-up gates and their rules, the pattern picker, landing prices and product names, the women's offer), which was replayed again in stage 3 with the same results; (2) how the older Manual app's engine worked in December 2025, which was read in the code twice; and (3) which exclusions Voy publishes. Do not read it as a map of Voy's consultation. No quiz screen was reached in any stage because of a security checkpoint that was deliberately not worked around, so there is no question list, no option-by-option rule and no observed recommendation for the real quiz. The rules that tie a medical answer to a product are published cautions or reasoning from them, now labelled as such, and several strengths and prices rest on search-engine summaries of pages that would not open. After the corrections above the labels are honest: 'observed' always has a run folder behind it, 'code' has been re-read in the file, 'docs' means 'Voy publishes this', and everything else is 'inferred' or 'unknown'.
topOpportunities: Give the verdict before asking for contact details, and never dead-end: for patchy, sudden or complete loss explain the likely causes and route to a clinician review, a GP letter or a dermatology referral.

Diagnose properly where Voy appears only to screen (its quiz could not be seen): ask about speed of loss, shedding, scalp symptoms, periods and menopause, recent illness, diet and medicines; use baseline photos reviewed by a clinician before the first prescription; offer ferritin, thyroid and hormone tests when the answers point that way.

Build a real women's pathway (cause work-up, topical and oral minoxidil at stated strengths, spironolactone and other anti-androgens where appropriate, menopause link, postpartum advice) instead of one medicine for every cause.

companies.parent: Skin + Me Ltd (sister services: Skin + Me, Renew + Me, Menopause + Me); medicines made and dispensed by Feel Good Pharma Ltd (The Feel Good Pharmacy), GPhC 9011329
companies.model: Subscription telehealth: one online questionnaire, review by pharmacist independent prescribers, then a personalised compounded hair-loss medicine (scalp drops or a once-a-day capsule) posted every four weeks at one flat price.
companies.accountWall: Step 'yd', 'Personalise your account' (legal first name, legal last name, preferred name), reached by pressing 'Continue to checkout' on the shopping bag. Everything before it works without an account: all medical questions, date of birth, the UK tick and the bag. The site silently creates an anonymous visitor id on arrival (POST /new-user) and saves each answer to it as you go.
companies.coverageNote: Stage 1 mapped both routes to the account wall. Stage 2 ran 14 replays: 2 baseline replays, 12 one-change experiments and 0 group tests of non-medical answers, each compared with a pool of baseline visits because the server varies screens at random. Covered one change at a time: first tile, age (17 years 11 months, 18, 85), pregnancy, five men's and six women's hair-loss pictures, recent onset, scalp infection and eczema, blood pressure (and its follow-up), eight further men's conditions, PCOS and heart disease for women, postpartum, facial hair, three medicine options, minoxidil allergy, previous finasteride, drops versus capsules on both routes, declining finasteride / dutasteride, pets, and a second goal. Everything after the legal-name screen (account, photos, payment, the prescriber's choice of formula, check-ins) was not tested and is described from public documents only.
companies.engineSummary: Hair + Me's public consultation collects answers; it does not decide anything a visitor can see. Stage 2 replayed it 14 times, changing one answer at a time (plus six group tests of non-medical answers), and compared every screen and the bag with a pool of baseline visits. Only a handful of answers do anything visible: sex at birth swaps the men's and women's question blocks; an age under 18 is the single hard stop; two or more goals, a blood-pressure diagnosis and 'pregnant, breastfeeding or likely to conceive' each add one screen; 'no hair loss' skips one; pets add a warning and a 'Better for pet owners' badge on The Capsules; previous treatments and 'Other' reveal a tick-box or a text box. Everything else, including patchy or sudden loss, an active scalp infection, heart disease, phaeochromocytoma, depression, prostate or breast cancer history, a minoxidil allergy, choosing drops over capsules and declining finasteride, leads to exactly the same screens and the same bag: 'Prescription · Personalised treatment · 4 week supply · 12ml', £34.99. The real engine is a pharmacist prescriber who, after account creation and payment, picks one of 16 compounded formulas (6 capsules, 10 drops). Its published limits are the leaflet contraindications: no finasteride or dutasteride for women; no oral minoxidil with heart disease, phaeochromocytoma or uncontrolled blood pressure; no finasteride or dutasteride with prostate, breast, sexual-function or mental-health history; no drops on an inflamed or infected scalp; only niacinamide drops in pregnancy or breastfeeding. Which strength a patient starts on is not published.
topOpportunities: Show the plan before the account wall: the likely medicine, strength and format, why it was chosen from the answers, and what was ruled out. Hair + Me shows one generic line to everyone, so a visible, explained recommendation is an immediate point of difference.

React to answers on screen. When someone ticks heart disease, uncontrolled blood pressure, a scalp infection or a minoxidil allergy, say at once what that means ('tablets are not suitable for you; here is what is') instead of staying silent until after payment.

Do real triage and be proud of it: route patchy, scarring-type or sudden loss to photos, a clinician call or a GP letter before any payment, and tell people with no hair loss that they do not need a prescription.
